Stiff Person Syndrome with Graves' Disease: A Rare Association
Sofia Junaid Syed, Khaldoun Haj Mahmoud, Miguel Chuquilin, Mariana Garcia-Touza
University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA
Introduction
Graves' disease is a common autoimmune disease that causes hyperthyroidism. Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS)
is a rare autoimmune neurologic disorder and is associated with anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies.

The patient is a 29 year-old male who was evaluated in endocrinology clinic after a recent admission to an inpatient psychiatry unit for suicidal attempt where he was found to have abnormal thyroid function tests.

The patient is a 29 year-old male who was evaluated in endocrinology clinic after a recent admission to an inpatient psychiatry unit for suicidal attempt where he was found to have abnormal thyroid function tests.
Initially his symptoms were occasional; however they had progressed over the last two years.
During this same time, the patient was also evaluated in the neurology clinic for spasticity and gait difficulty with a limp in the left lower extremity.
Due to his history of back and leg spasms, increased muscle tone and positive GAD antibodies, the patient was diagnosed with SPS and prescribed baclofen with good improvement in spasticity.
